item.title: Nvidia Chief, Jensen Huang, Is Seen as Target of Chinese Spy Plot
item.description: A Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang was found to be passing intelligence to Beijing. President Trump was briefed and took no action.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Swan, Maggie Haberman, Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Tripp Mickle and Julian E. Barnes
item.category: Far East, South and Southeast Asia and Pacific Areas
item.media:credit: Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times
item.media:description: Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, is influential at the White House on technology policy and has developed a close relationship with President Trump.

item.title: At Least 68 Killed in Spain Train Crash, and Democrats’ Secret Effort to Stack Alaska’s Ballot
item.description: Plus, the legacy of Dolores Huerta.
item.dc:creator: Tracy Mumford, Will Jarvis, Margaret Kadifa, Jake Lucas, Ian Stewart, Kellen Browning and Manny Fernandez

item.title: U.S. GDP Increased 3.4% in Third Quarter
item.description: The economy grew 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year. Strong spending and growth contrast with the poor marks that many voters are giving the economy.
item.dc:creator: Ben Casselman

item.title: Inflation Accelerated in October, PCE Index Shows
item.description: The Personal Consumption Expenditures index picked up in September, according to data released a day after the Federal Reserve’s decision to hold interest rates steady.
item.dc:creator: Aruni Soni
item.media:description: A factor pushing prices up this year has been a severe energy crunch created by the war with Iran that sent oil prices soaring.

item.title: In Moving Gradually, Fed Risks Having to Play Catch-Up to Quell Inflation
item.description: Federal Reserve officials are expected to restart rate increases in December, but the cadence of additional moves will depend on the data.
item.dc:creator: Colby Smith
item.media:description: Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaking on Wednesday.

item.title: Alaska Governor Orders Criminal Investigation Into Peltola Campaign
item.description: President Trump had lashed out at Mary Peltola after The New York Times reported that her campaign and national Democrats helped recruit spoiler candidates to the race. He offered no explanation of what crime may have been committed.
item.dc:creator: Kellen Browning and Anna Griffin
item.media:description: President Trump campaigned this month for Senator Dan S. Sullivan of Alaska, a Republican running for re-election this year against Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former congresswoman.

item.title: The Red States That Could Decide the Senate
item.description: Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to regain the majority, but some of their targets are in states President Trump won by double digits in 2024. Our election data reporter Evan Reynolds explains just how difficult that might be.
item.dc:creator: Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, June Kim, Sutton Raphael and Thomas Vollkommer

item.title: As Trump Faces Down the Midterms, a Grim Mood Takes Over the White House
item.description: The White House has been rocked by turnover and anxiety over the midterms. The president, who is tightening his inner circle, has lashed out at critics, held meandering rallies and feasted on a diet of news clips and “A.I. slop,” as one aide put it.
item.dc:creator: Katie Rogers
item.media:description: President Trump after a campaign rally in Mississippi on Monday.

item.title: Cabinet Officials on the Campaign Trail? Ethics Experts Say Some Are Breaking the Law.
item.description: As Trump officials stump for Republican candidates facing difficult races, ethics experts say they are being lax about complying with the Hatch Act, a federal anti-corruption law.
item.dc:creator: Karoun Demirjian
item.media:description: President Trump with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at a campaign rally in North Carolina this month.

item.title: After 28 Years Walking the Globe, Karl Bushby Is Almost Home
item.description: Karl Bushby has walked 31,000 miles, crossing some of the world’s harshest landscapes. He plans to reach his mother’s house in England next week.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Wolfe
item.media:credit: Sam Bush for The New York Times
item.media:description: Mr. Bushby in London. He said his journey was a reminder of people’s kindness.

item.title: How Netanyahu Used Fear, Again, to Win More Votes Than Anyone Else
item.description: Despite years of political baggage, the Israeli prime minister outperformed expectations, and his rivals, by playing on Jewish voters’ fears of Arab political power and potential security threats.
item.dc:creator: David M. Halbfinger
item.media:description: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reacts to exit polls during a speech at his party headquarters in Jerusalem on Wednesday.

item.title: With No Clear Winner, How Could Israel Get a Prime Minister?
item.description: Deadlock is possible, as neither the bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main challenger appear likely to win a majority. But there are still paths to a new government.
item.dc:creator: Johnatan Reiss, Adina Renner and Pablo Robles

item.title: How Arab Voters in Israel Shifted the Political Landscape
item.description: The Arab parties have long been kept on the political sidelines. But stunning turnout by their supporters makes the Arab minority an Israeli political reality that cannot be ignored.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Boxerman
item.media:description: Voting in the predominantly Arab town of Tayibe during the Israeli election on Tuesday.

item.title: A Ukrainian City in the Kill Zone Relishes a Moment of Peace
item.description: A rare localized cease-fire announced by the first lady, Melania Trump, offered a brief respite for Kherson, where Russian drones and artillery have long terrorized civilians.
item.dc:creator: Siobhán O’Grady, Liubov Sholudko and David Guttenfelder
item.media:description: Net covered streets in Kherson protect against Russian drone assaults as people take advantage of the relative calm during a local, temporary cease-fire on Wednesday, set up to allow the upcoming evacuation of civilians from neighboring town of Oleshky.

item.title: Russian Strike on Ukrainian Train Station Kills 14
item.description: A deadly strike was a grim reminder that despite a rare local cease-fire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, other communities remained under fire.
item.dc:creator: Cassandra Vinograd
item.media:credit: Agence France-Presse, via Ukrainian Emergency Service
item.media:description: A photo released by the Ukrainian Emergency Service after an air attack on a railway station in Dnipro, Ukraine, on Thursday.

item.title: Ilhan Omar Investigation Involves New Scrutiny of Long-Disputed Marriage
item.description: Several current and former law enforcement officials said an Obama-era investigation found some evidence that Ms. Omar had entered into a sham marriage with a man suspected of being her brother.
item.dc:creator: Ernesto Londoño
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times
item.media:description: Representative Ilhan Omar at the Capitol in Washington earlier this year.

item.title: The Five-Borough Route: The Beating Heart of the NYC Marathon
item.description: When the event’s five co-founders first proposed moving it out of Central Park, it seemed impossible. Much has changed in the sport and the city since that 1976 race.
item.dc:creator: Jennie Coughlin
item.media:description: Runners on the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge during the 1976 New York City Marathon, the first to include all five boroughs.

item.title: At NYC Marathon, Cowbells Are a Signature Sound. But Why?
item.description: Screaming fans and clanging cowbells have become the soundtrack to the New York City Marathon and to sporting events around the world.
item.dc:creator: Claire Fahy
item.media:credit: Graham Dickie for The New York Times
item.media:description: Fans at the 2025 New York City Marathon.

item.title: New York City Marathon Weather Forecast: Warmer Temperatures Than Normal
item.description: Thousands of runners will take part in the New York City Marathon on Sunday. Temperatures are expected to be unusually warm for November.
item.dc:creator: Nazaneen Ghaffar
item.media:credit: Johnny Milano for The New York Times
item.media:description: Runners in the New York City Marathon in 2022 faced unusually high temperatures.

item.title: Spain Crash Investigators Focus on Train Traffic Controllers’ Role
item.description: After the country’s second major rail disaster in a year, Spaniards were confronting questions about the safety of their once-vaunted rail system.
item.dc:creator: Jason Horowitz
item.media:description: Emergency workers were still searching for survivors and victims at the site of the crash on Thursday.

item.title: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as President of European Central Bank
item.description: Her plan to depart in February, months before the end of an eight-year term, sets in motion a selection process among European leaders for a new central bank president.
item.dc:creator: Eshe Nelson
item.media:description: Christine Lagarde’s appointment as the European Central Bank’s first woman president was the latest step in a career of breaking gender barriers, while also contending with economic crises.
